title: Rox raises $100M Series B at $1.3B for enterprise sales agents
subtitle: General Catalyst and March Capital co-led, with Databricks Ventures and Prosperity7 as new investors — the latest in a wave of unicorn-scale Series Bs for agent startups.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Rox, a San Francisco AI startup, said on November 11 that it had raised $100 million in a Series B valuing the company at $1.3 billion. General Catalyst and March Capital co-led the round, with participation from existing investors Sequoia Capital and Factory and new investors Databricks Ventures and Prosperity7 Ventures. Rox builds autonomous agents aimed at enterprise sales teams — generating leads, booking meetings, moving deals and expanding accounts inside existing CRM systems. The company said it will use the capital to advance AI research, develop custom models and expand its customer base across healthcare, industrial, financial services, energy and technology.

The number matters because of what it says about how the market is pricing agent companies. Rox's prior round in March valued it at $1.2 billion, and the Series B lifts it only modestly — meaning investors paid for execution, not multiple expansion. The company is pitched as a direct challenger to Salesforce's existing seat of enterprise sales workflow, which is the clearest competitive line any AI agent startup has drawn in 2026.

Rox sits inside a crowded field of enterprise agent startups raising at near-unicorn or unicorn valuations. Serval closed $150 million at a $3 billion valuation in early November. Reflection AI is nearing a round that would value it at up to $5.5 billion. Cognition hit $47 billion in September on $1 billion of ARR. The shared bet is that horizontal foundation models will be wrapped in company-specific orchestration, and that whichever startup wins the wrapper for a given business function will own a durable interface. Series B activity more broadly is down 26% per one roundup, but AI agent rounds have been immune so far.

A takeaway for learners: a $1.3 billion valuation on a Series B used to be a late-stage number. It is now, increasingly, a signal that the market has chosen a bet before the bet has shown revenue proof. That changes how to read these announcements. The information in a round size is mostly about the market's confidence in the category, not about the specific company — separate those two when the next headline lands.
